\title{A Monitor's AUROC Is Not Evidence the Monitor Works:\\
Reading vs.\ Writing a Correctness Probe}

\begin{abstract}
A linear correctness probe on a small language model's hidden states reaches held-out AUROC $0.982$ and, as a best-of-16 selector, captures $88.8\%$ of the headroom available to \emph{any} selector --- a monitor a practitioner would deploy. Promoting a monitor to the RL reward is catastrophic: true accuracy falls $31$\,pp while the reward monitor's own score climbs to $0.99$, and our objective contains \textbf{no evasion term}, so the policy is complying rather than concealing. \emph{That reward is a separate temp-1 probe, not the $0.982$ probe above; the two share a direction at cosine $0.163$.} Within a single frozen artifact the asymmetry is sharper still: a 39-feature surface monitor reads at AUROC $\mathbf{0.925}$ and, as the reward, drives accuracy to exactly $\mathbf{0.0000}$ with $99.9\%$ of rollouts still well-formed. Ranked on one population, read-only quality orders the three rewards \textbf{backwards}: $0.834 \to 0.168$, $0.861 \to 0.073$, $0.925 \to 0.000$. A better reader is not a safer writer. Scoring the frozen monitor at every checkpoint against \emph{that checkpoint's own} rollouts  we find the hacking precedes the monitor's failure by $\sim$\textbf{40 RLOO steps}: its AUROC is flat while the policy is already gaming it. Repeating the identical measurement with an \textbf{LLM judge} on the same checkpoints, its AUROC dips $0.031$ at step 30 ($p=0.002$) and recovers, ending where it began ($0.785 \to 0.769$; the paired change is $-0.017$ with $95\%$ CI $[-0.048, +0.014]$, which rules out degradation beyond about $0.05$ rather than merely failing to reject zero) across a 32-point accuracy collapse. Its operating point does not degrade either: the prevalence-invariant likelihood ratio $\mathrm{LR}+$ ends where it began ($2.46 \to 2.57$), while the frozen monitor's collapses to $1.00$ --- chance. What moves is the one statistic needing \textbf{no labels}: the fraction of rollouts passed at a frozen threshold ($-37\%$ for the judge; $+38\%$ for the probe by step 40, against AUROC's $-5\%$ of its above-chance margin). It departs significantly from its frozen value at the first checkpoint measured (step 10, $p<0.001$ paired), $\sim$40 steps before AUROC breaks --- an ordering we demonstrate rather than calibrate, on a control we document the limits of. \textbf{Monitor where your evaluator's score distribution sits relative to the threshold you froze} --- it is the only diagnostic here that survives not having a verifier, which is the situation that motivates deploying a judge in the first place. We then price how much of the collapse is confound occupation with an instrument that costs nothing: a monitor reading only cheap text features reproduces the failure signature, and as the reward destroys the task outright, with $99.9\%$ of rollouts still emitting well-formed but arithmetic-free answers. Read-only monitor quality does not transfer to gradient-facing use, and AUROC does not tell you which regime you are in.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Linear probes on hidden states are increasingly proposed as control signals --- refusal directions \citep{arditi2024refusal}, correctness probes \citep{burns2022discovering}, deception probes \citep{pacchiardi2023lie} --- and the natural next step, wiring one into the RL loop, is much less well understood than using it read-only. Two literatures bear on this. Reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling, coste2023reward, skalse2022defining, denison2024sycophancy} shows that externally-trained proxy rewards Goodhart under gradient access, with no adversarial term anywhere. Monitor evasion \citep{baker2025monitoring, gupta2025rlobfuscation, taufeeque2026atlas, bailey2024obfuscated} shows that latent-space monitors can be evaded when they enter as a \emph{penalty}. A third literature, on LLM evaluators \citep{zheng2023judging}, has converged independently on our thesis from the measurement side: accuracy and agreement overstate judge reliability \citep{norman2026reliability, weng2026invariance}, judge scores move when only the judge changes \citep{yang2026auditing}, and the link from reward-model benchmark scores to downstream RLHF outcomes is weak enough to have needed purpose-built benchmarks to establish \citep{frick2024ppe, malik2025rewardbench2}. We add the dynamic case: what those statistics do \emph{while} the policy they watch is degrading. \textbf{We claim neither mechanism as novel.} Our instantiation --- an internal probe on the policy's own activations, as a positive reward --- is the closest analogue to how interpretability artifacts are actually being proposed as control signals, and it yields one consequence worth stating: collapse without an evasion term means auditing for adversarial pressure is not sufficient.

Our substantive contribution is a measurement. \citet{baker2025monitoring} report monitor recall collapsing under optimization pressure but cannot separate \emph{the agent evaded} from \emph{the monitor stopped discriminating}, because the two are not measured on held-apart data. An exactly-verifiable task lets us separate them at every checkpoint, on that checkpoint's own rollouts --- and the answer is that a monitor's health statistics are the last thing to move. This is the mirror image of \citet{beigi2026prime}, who show that probing a policy \emph{internally} forecasts hack onset before the visible hack rate rises: the information is there to be read, but not in the monitor's own accuracy against its target. We show this for a linear probe and then for an LLM judge, and identify the one diagnostic that survives not having a verifier.

We work on Qwen2.5-0.5B trained on Countdown arithmetic \citep{gandhi2024stream} with RLOO \citep{ahmadian2024back}: an exact verifier, so a learned scorer's divergence from ground truth is measurable without preference-model confounds.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{Read-only quality does not transfer to gradient-facing use.} A trace-final probe reaches held-out AUROC $0.982$ and captures $88.8\%$ of best-of-16 headroom. Promoted to the reward it costs $31$\,pp; a frozen surface monitor reading at $0.925$ costs everything, driving accuracy to $0.0000$. Scored on one population, the three rewards are ordered \emph{inversely} to their read-only quality ($0.834 \to 0.168$, $0.861 \to 0.073$, $0.925 \to 0.000$), so read-only quality does not order the outcomes. (\S\ref{sec:probe-reader}, \S\ref{sec:probe-rl}, \S\ref{sec:surface})
  \item \textbf{Monitor health statistics move last.} Scored at every checkpoint against that checkpoint's own rollouts, the probe's AUROC is indistinguishable from its starting value through step 40 ($p=0.22$) and breaks only at 50 --- while the policy has been gaming it since step 10. (\S\ref{sec:lag})
  \item \textbf{The same measurement on an LLM judge}, where AUROC dips $0.031$ and recovers, and the prevalence-adjusted operating point does not degrade at all across a $31.7$\,pp accuracy collapse. (\S\ref{sec:judge})
  \item \textbf{The one diagnostic that needs no labels.} Flag rate at a frozen threshold departs significantly at step 10, $\sim$40 steps before AUROC breaks. Every other statistic here requires the ground truth a deployed evaluator lacks. (\S\ref{sec:lag})
\end{enumerate}

\section{Setup}\label{sec:setup}

Qwen2.5-0.5B on Countdown (given 3--4 integers and a target, produce an equation using each exactly once; an exact rule-based verifier returns $\{0,0.1,1.0\}$). $C_{\text{SFT}}$ is \texttt{asingh15/qwen-sft-countdown-defaultproj}; $C_{\text{outcome}}$ is 100 RLOO \citep{ahmadian2024back} steps with the verifier reward (batch 128, KL $10^{-3}$, lr $10^{-5}$), taking pass@1 from $28.6\%$ to $53.5\%$. Eval is 500 procedurally generated problems filtered to the 406 with no overlap against the RLOO training pool. Probes are L2-regularized logistic regression at layer 16, 5-fold \texttt{GroupKFold} on prompt, class-balanced. \textbf{One estimator throughout:} cross-validate then balance, held out by prompt; where an in-sample figure exists we do not quote it (the trace-final probe reads $0.995$ in-sample against $0.982$ held out). Balanced AUROC is seed-dependent at the $\sim$0.015 level, so we do not lean on a third decimal.

\section{The monitor is genuinely good}\label{sec:probe-reader}

A trace-final probe on layer-16 \texttt{</think>} hidden states reaches held-out AUROC $\mathbf{0.982}$ on $C_{\text{outcome}}$, and is operationally useful: as a best-of-16 selector on 406 held-out prompts it reaches $0.6700$ against a random-pick baseline of $0.5531$ and an oracle ceiling of $0.6847$, capturing $88.8\%$ of the available headroom (prompt-clustered paired bootstrap, CI $[78.9\%, 96.5\%]$). We state the free baselines beside it because they are close: \texttt{</think>} \emph{position alone} --- one regex, no forward pass --- scores AUROC $0.915$ and selects at $0.6379$, and a 39-feature surface model scores $0.926$. The probe's margin is $+0.056$ AUROC and $+3.20$ pp of selection accuracy (CI $[+0.99,+5.42]$, $p=0.008$). It is a good detector that partly rides on a cheap surface correlate, and \S\ref{sec:surface} is where that matters. High probe accuracy is not by itself evidence that the model \emph{uses} the direction \citep{belinkov2022probing}; we make no causal claim about it here. Two disclosures: rollouts with no locatable \texttt{</think>} are unscoreable and excluded from every AUROC ($2.9\%$ on $C_{\text{outcome}}$, $10.4\%$ on $C_{\text{SFT}}$, all wrong, so the filter flatters the weaker checkpoint); and layer 16 was fixed in advance from the original study, not selected here. \paragraph{We pre-empt the length objection rather than waiting for it.} A reviewer will ask whether the probe is reading trace length. It partly is, and the honest shape of the answer is in the table: a free structural baseline already captures $64\%$ of the headroom. But the probe beats it --- \textbf{probe $-$ shortest-\texttt{<think>} $= +3.20$\,pp}, 95\% CI $[+0.99, +5.42]$, $p = 0.008$ --- and beats the strongest free baseline we could construct, a 39-feature surface model, by the same $+3.20$\,pp ($p = 0.004$). Combined with AUROC $0.939$ under position stratification (against $0.564$ for position alone), the probe is not a length detector; it is a good detector that partly rides on length.

\noindent \textbf{One probe or two.} The probe promoted to reward, and scored at every checkpoint in \S\ref{sec:lag}, is a temp-1 fit whose own held-out AUROC is $\mathbf{0.810}$ under its own label rule and split --- \emph{not} the $0.982$ trace-final probe above, whose direction it shares only at cosine $0.163$. To rank it against the two reward arms of \S\ref{sec:surface} we must score it on \emph{their} population, and restricted to the $158$ prompts it was never fit on it reads $\mathbf{0.861}$ (0.850 if we additionally intersect the arms' own held-out half). That is the only figure we use when ranking rewards; $0.810$ and $0.982$ are not comparable to it or to each other. \textbf{One disclosure we owe on the lag ladder.} $248$ of this probe's $300$ fitting prompts are among the $406$ evaluated in \S\ref{sec:lag}, so that evaluation is \emph{not} prompt-disjoint from the probe's fit. Rollouts are freshly sampled at every checkpoint, and the probe's step-0 reading of $0.783$ sits \emph{below} its held-out $0.810$ rather than above it, which is not the direction leakage produces --- but the populations do overlap, and we state that rather than resting the ladder on a disjointness we do not have. The lag result is about an $0.810$ monitor.

\section{Writing through the probe in RL fails catastrophically}\label{sec:probe-rl}

What happens if we promote the probe to a writer --- the optimization target of an RL training run? We tested this in two initialization regimes, each 100 RLOO steps with identical hyperparameters to vanilla outcome RL:
\begin{description}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
  \item[\texttt{runA}] Init from $C_{\text{outcome}}$ (probe in-distribution at step 0).
  \item[\texttt{runB}] Init from $C_{\text{SFT}}$ (probe cross-distribution at step 0).
\end{description}
The reward is the probe's $P(\text{correct})$, read at \texttt{</think>} of a frozen reference reloaded each round. The verifier is logged but does not enter the gradient.

\paragraph{Downstream eval.} On the clean-406 eval set (first-block accuracy), the same population as every other table here:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Checkpoint & first-block accuracy & vs.\ same-init baseline \\
\midrule
$C_{\text{outcome}}$ (vanilla RLOO from $C_{\text{SFT}}$) & $0.550$ & --- \\
\textbf{probe-RL \texttt{runA}} (from $C_{\text{outcome}}$) & \textbf{0.236} & $-31$\,pp from $C_{\text{outcome}}$ \\
\textbf{probe-RL \texttt{runB}} (from $C_{\text{SFT}}$, baseline $0.290$) & \textbf{0.073} & $-22$\,pp from $C_{\text{SFT}}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\paragraph{What the attacked policy emits.} A transparent template-match score over the rollout text (distinct markers from ``let me'', ``step by step'', ``therefore'', ``the answer is'', a verification-language family, a numbered-step pattern, sequential markers) rises $2.00 \to 4.32$ out of 7 between the vanilla checkpoint and \texttt{runB}; its correlation with correctness collapses from $r{=}{+}0.320$ to $+0.025$; and $100\%$ of attacked rollouts carry template score $\geq 3$ against $15.1\%$ at baseline. The rhetorical form is fully decoupled from the mathematics while the probe still scores it correct. The two runs adopted \emph{opposite} exploits --- \texttt{runA} rambles, \texttt{runB} commits early --- both reaching probe $\approx 0.99$.

\subsection{The monitor's AUROC is intact for 40 steps after the hacking starts}\label{sec:lag}

Because the monitor is a \emph{verifiable} correctness probe, we can do something the reward-model literature structurally cannot: measure the monitor's discrimination on the current policy's own distribution at every checkpoint, for free. A reward model would need fresh preference labels at each step; a correctness probe needs only the verifier we already have. We harvest all eleven checkpoints of the probe-as-reward run and, at each, sample 8 fresh rollouts per prompt \emph{from that checkpoint} and score the frozen reward probe against ground truth. Nothing is held fixed across checkpoints except the probe.

Band is the across-seed range of the class-balanced AUROC. The verifier-RL control (dashed) \emph{rises} over the same interval, so the decline is specific to the attacked checkpoint and not something training does to a frozen probe.}

\textbf{Which metric warns you.} AUROC is rank-based, so it is invariant to monotone recalibration --- and steps 0--40 are close to exactly that, the score inflating $0.460 \to 0.677$ while preserving order. ``AUROC stayed flat'' is therefore partly a property of the metric, and the same holds for every rank-based evaluator statistic including TPR at fixed FPR. The obvious replacement is confounded: raw precision at a frozen threshold falls $0.588 \to 0.416$ ($-29.3\%$), and the base rate falls with it. Removing prevalence does not shrink that: the prevalence-invariant $\mathrm{LR}+$ falls $2.41 \to 1.65$, $\mathbf{-31.5\%}$, slightly \emph{more} than the raw number advertises. We use $\mathrm{LR}+$ and not \emph{lift} here for the reason \S\ref{sec:judge} sets out: lift is not prevalence-invariant, and on this series it moves only $-12.8\%$. Measured against its above-chance margin, AUROC moves $-5.1\%$ over the same span.

\textbf{Which label-free readout works.} AUROC, precision and lift all need current ground truth --- and with that you could measure the accuracy drop directly. What remains with no labels at all? Score \emph{saturation} fails: the attacked run has $36.7\%$ of rollouts above $0.95$ by step 40, but the verifier-RL control reaches $37.2\%$ by step 60 \emph{while its accuracy rises}. \textbf{Flag rate works.} The fraction above the frozen threshold rises monotonically under attack ($+6\%,+12\%,+20\%,\mathbf{+38\%}$ at steps 10--40, reaching $+99\%$) and never returns. Because every checkpoint is scored on the same 406 prompts, the right test is the paired one, and it is decisive at the \emph{first} checkpoint after training begins: $+0.030\,[+0.012,+0.048]$ at \textbf{step 10} ($p<0.001$; no bootstrap draw of 2{,}000 crossed zero), against an AUROC break at 50. That is a label-free lead of $\sim$\textbf{40 steps}. Every subsequent checkpoint is also significant, and the effect grows monotonically to $+0.496$ by step 99. A paired test against step 0 establishes that the statistic \emph{moved}, not that it moved more than benign training moves it; for that we need a control, and ours is weak. \textbf{This control is the weakest link in the paper and we state its defects rather than its width.} It has five checkpoints; it initialises from $C_{\mathrm{SFT}}$ rather than $C_{\mathrm{outcome}}$, the init mismatch we insist on elsewhere; its manifest records no sampling configuration, because it was ingested from earlier evaluations rather than harvested by the pipeline used for the attacked ladder; and, decisively, its three mid-series checkpoints are scored on 166--167 prompts where every attacked checkpoint uses all 406. The $\pm 18.6\%$ band is set by exactly the checkpoint where that population changes. Restricting to the two population-matched checkpoints gives $\pm 5.1\%$, which the attacked run leaves at step 10 --- agreeing with the paired test above, and making step 30 the outlier estimate rather than the safe one, since it is the contaminated band that produces it. Two independent routes give step 10; only the artifact-laden one gives 30. Read the lead as a demonstration that the ordering exists, not as a calibrated false-alarm rate: a properly matched control ladder is the single highest-value experiment left undone here. In the judge experiment the same statistic moves $-37\%$ --- the opposite sign --- so what to watch for is \emph{departure} from the frozen operating point, not a direction. We claim the RL-training characterisation of this alarm, not the alarm: watching a score distribution against a frozen reference is standard practice in production monitoring, and \citet{li2026whodrifted} give a strictly better instrument for it --- anytime-valid e-processes with an anchor set, which additionally attribute drift to the system or to the judge. Our contribution is to price what that alarm buys you in RLOO steps against a monitor whose AUROC has not yet moved.

\subsection{The same measurement on an actual LLM judge}\label{sec:judge}

The monitor above is a linear probe. A reader at this venue should want to know whether any of it survives contact with the object they actually deploy, so we repeat the measurement with an LLM judge and change nothing else.

We re-sample all eleven checkpoints of the same run (406 prompts $\times$ 8 rollouts, 35{,}728 rollouts) and score every rollout twice: with the exact verifier, and with \texttt{Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct} shown the problem and the proposed equation and asked whether it is correct. The judge's score is $P(\textsc{yes})$ renormalised over the two verdict tokens. It is a genuinely imperfect judge --- at step 0 it scores $0.746$ precision at its own median threshold against a true accuracy of $0.544$ --- which is the point: this is what a deployed evaluator looks like.

\textbf{The judge's AUROC dips and recovers; end to end it does not move} (Table~\ref{tab:judge}). Paired prompt-clustered bootstraps --- the right test, since every checkpoint is scored on the same 406 prompts --- show a small but significant dip at steps 20--40 ($-0.031$ at step 30, $p = 0.002$), a recovery by step 80 ($+0.038$ from step 30, $p = 0.012$, though steps 30 and 80 are the observed argmin and argmax, so we report that contrast as exploratory), and \emph{no} difference between the first and last checkpoints ($p = 0.31$). The series is non-monotone, so quoting first-versus-last would read the least sensitive contrast off a U shape; we give all eleven. The largest excursion, $0.031$ AUROC, arrives while true accuracy is falling $0.544 \to 0.457$ and would not trip any plausible alert.

\textbf{Its operating point does not degrade at all once prevalence is removed.} Step 0 and step 99 are $0.785\,[0.757,0.813]$ and $0.769\,[0.737,0.801]$. Raw precision at a threshold frozen on the step-0 distribution falls $0.746 \to 0.429$, which looks like a $42\%$ collapse --- but the base rate falls $0.544 \to 0.226$ over the same span, and precision at a fixed threshold is confounded with prevalence by construction. The prevalence-invariant statistic is the positive likelihood ratio $\mathrm{LR}+ = \mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR}$, and it is flat end to end: $\mathbf{2.46 \to 2.57}$, with the same shallow mid-training dip as AUROC ($2.22$ at step 30). We flag one trap we fell into ourselves: \emph{lift} (precision over base rate) is \textbf{not} prevalence-invariant, since $\mathrm{lift}=\mathrm{TPR}/[b\,\mathrm{TPR}+(1{-}b)\mathrm{FPR}]$. Holding this judge's step-0 TPR and FPR fixed and moving only the base rate $0.544 \to 0.226$ predicts lift $1.37 \to 1.85$, against $1.90$ observed --- so lift's apparent $38\%$ ``improvement'' is $\sim$92\% the very confound we set out to remove. We report this because we made the error ourselves first, and it is the same structure \citet{norman2026reliability} document at scale for judge agreement: exact-match agreement flatters a judge, and the chance-corrected version deflates by as much as 33--41\,pp. A base-rate correction changing the sign of an evaluator's apparent trend is not a curiosity of our setup.

\textbf{So the honest result is the uncomfortable one, and it is not that the judge held up.} The judge is a \emph{fixed function}: of the 965 (problem, equation) pairs it scored more than once, exactly one changes which side of the threshold it falls on, and of the 48 it scored at both step 0 and step 99, none do. Its AUROC was therefore never measuring the thing that broke. What changed is the distribution it was handed, in composition --- correct answers fall from $54.4\%$ of the pool to $22.6\%$, illegal ones growing from $28\%$ of the wrong answers to $43\%$ --- and in surface form: the policy stops using parentheses, the share of correct answers with none rising $0.017 \to 0.982$, and on the same expression differing only in bracketing the judge passes $0.746$ with parentheses against $0.548$ without ($+0.198$, $95\%$ CI $[+0.131, +0.265]$). That is the paper's own thesis turned on the judge: it too is riding a surface correlate. The per-answer rates in Table~\ref{tab:errors} move for that reason and not because the judge improved or decayed --- sensitivity and specificity belong to a classifier \emph{and a population together}. A flat AUROC here is not evidence the judge is healthy; its health was never the variable. Nothing in its own label-requiring statistics would have told you the policy was failing.

\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
 & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{share of answers}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{judge passes them}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-4}\cmidrule(lr){5-7}
what the model produced & step 0 & step 50 & step 99 & step 0 & step 50 & step 99 \\
\midrule
correct                        & 0.544 & 0.399 & \textbf{0.226} & 0.686 & 0.590 & 0.600 \\
legal equation, wrong value    & 0.294 & 0.316 & 0.442 & 0.408 & 0.412 & \textbf{0.399} \\
uses numbers it was not given  & 0.129 & 0.284 & 0.330 & 0.057 & 0.025 & 0.013 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{What the judge was shown, and how it responded. The left half is the mix of answers; the right half is the judge's pass rate on each kind. The judge itself is a fixed function, so the right-hand movement reflects the answers changing form, not the judge changing. A fourth bucket, answers with no parseable equation, is always rejected and shrinks $3.3\% \to 0.2\%$; it is omitted, so the shares sum to under one.}
\label{tab:errors}
\end{table} Both AUROC and precision need current ground truth; with that in hand you could measure the accuracy drop directly, and it is louder than either. What moves without labels is the flag rate: $0.500 \to 0.317$ ($-37\%$) against AUROC's $-2\%$, and it departs significantly at step 20 ($-0.026\,[-0.047,-0.007]$, $p=0.013$; step 10 is not significant, $p=0.069$), and it is not monotone, bottoming at $0.294$ by step 80 before drifting back to $0.317$ while accuracy still falls. Note the sign is opposite to the probe's: what to watch is \emph{departure} from the frozen operating point, not a direction.

\textbf{Two scope limits we state rather than let a reader find.} First, the judge is a \emph{bystander}: the policy was optimised against the probe, never against the judge, so this is not a demonstration that a judge can be gamed. That contrast is instructive: \citet{zhou2026convincing} optimise \emph{against} reference-free judges in self-play and report pass rate climbing $0.72 \to 0.94$ over a true accuracy flat at $0.20$, with even a three-judge cross-family ensemble's discrimination (TPR$-$FPR) collapsing $0.311 \to 0.086$. A judge under direct optimisation loses discrimination; a bystander judge, we find, keeps it while the policy collapses underneath. The failure is the same --- neither judge's own statistics warn you --- but only one is an evasion story. It is the weaker and more common situation --- an evaluator watching a policy that is drifting for reasons of its own --- and it is the one a practitioner is usually in. Second, the two AUROC series are scored against different label conventions (the probe against last-block correctness, the label it was fit on; the judge against the first answer block, which is what it is shown), so the curves are each correct on their own terms but should not be read as a like-for-like overlay. The judge result above does not depend on the comparison.

\subsection{How much of the collapse is surface occupation?}\label{sec:surface}

A frozen detector reading nothing but \texttt{</think>} character position --- threshold set on \emph{correct baseline} rollouts, never refit --- loses almost all its precision on the attacked policy ($83.1\% \to 16.0\%$) while flagging an unchanged share of rollouts ($30.1\% \to 29.7\%$). A seven-feature text-only logistic regression, frozen on baseline, reproduces the probe's signature: its mean $P(\text{correct})$ rises $0.506 \to 0.832$ while true accuracy falls $0.517 \to 0.130$. So a monitor with no access to the model's internals inherits the failure.

We then closed the loop with two pre-registered RL arms (predictions committed before launch), same recipe as the published run, both initialised from $C_{\text{SFT}}$ and compared against the init-matched run \texttt{runB} at $0.0734$, which we list as arm C. \textbf{The AUROC column is one population and one label rule} --- the clean-406 $C_{\text{outcome}}$ rollouts, each probe scored only on prompts it was not fit on --- so the three are rankable against each other and against nothing else in this paper. Rows are sorted by read-only quality, and the accuracy column runs the other way:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Arm & reward & read-only AUROC & first-block acc.\ (vs.\ \texttt{runB}) \\
\midrule
A & surface-\emph{residualised} probe & 0.834 & $0.1678$ \ \ ($+9.44$ pp, CI $[+7.67,+11.24]$) \\
C & the raw probe (\texttt{runB}, reference) & 0.861 & $0.0734$ \ \ (reference) \\
B & surface features \emph{only} & 0.925 & $\mathbf{0.0000}$ \ \ ($-7.34$ pp, CI $[-8.41,-6.31]$) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Arm B is the sharpest artifact here.} A reward with no access to the model's internals whatsoever drove accuracy to exactly zero --- and the failure is not degenerate output, which is what makes it informative: $100\%$ of rollouts still emit \texttt{</think>} and $99.9\%$ a well-formed \texttt{<answer>} block. Verbatim, for input $[29, 17, 63, 38]$, target $68$:

\begin{quote}\ttfamily\small
<answer>\\
Let me verify:\\
1. 17 - 10 = 7\\
2. 63 - 7 = 56\\
3. 29 * 38 = 1102\\
4. 56 - (29 * 38 / 38) = 68\\
</answer>
\end{quote}

Step 1 uses \texttt{10}, not in the input. Step 3 is correct and irrelevant. Step 4 reuses two numbers and evaluates to 27 --- while \emph{asserting} 68 in the answer position. The rollout has the shape of careful verification and contains no valid arithmetic. Mean length went $1{,}098 \to 2{,}390$ characters: the policy learned to fill the answer slot with more correct-\emph{looking} work, because \texttt{ans\_len}, \texttt{ans\_ops} and \texttt{n\_equals} reward exactly that.

Arm A \emph{confirmed} its pre-registered prediction against the init-matched control, collapsing $9.4$ pp less than the raw-probe run. We note the earlier cross-initialisation comparison (against \texttt{runA}, from $C_{\text{outcome}}$) reversed this sign, and that initialisation is worth $\sim$16 pp here on its own --- more than twice the effect --- which is why the contrast must match on it.

\paragraph{What this licenses, and what it does not.} Licensed: occupying cheap textual structure is \emph{sufficient} to destroy both a monitor and the task, with no internal access required. Not licensed: that this is \emph{the} mechanism of the published probe's collapse --- Arm A cuts against the simple version of that story. The prescription is narrower and we think more useful: before wiring any monitor into a gradient, measure how much of its AUROC survives conditioning on cheap surface features. Our probe holds $0.982 \to 0.939$ under \texttt{</think>}-position stratification, so it carries real signal beyond the surface, and it still collapsed --- because the \emph{policy's} accessible axes are the surface ones. Read-only quality is necessary and not sufficient; the question is not what the monitor can see, it is what the optimizer can reach.

\paragraph{Bounding gradient access buys very little.} Three constructions bound the probe's gradient access rather than removing it: a target-invariant leave-one-out control variate (Goodhart-free by construction, untested), multiplicative shaping $r=\text{verifier}\times\text{probe}$ ($+2.84$\,pp), and probe-best-of-$K$ selection ($+1.5$\,pp; blocks per rollout $1.83 \to 0.91$). Each is one training run, and their intervals are over prompts rather than runs --- the vanilla baseline moves 4--6\,pp between adjacent late checkpoints of a single run, which exceeds both effects. Against read-only selection's $+11.7$\,pp, \textbf{nothing we tried that puts the probe in the training loop outperforms not putting it there.}

\section{Limitations}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{Every RL configuration is one seed}, including the ladder the lag is measured on. The three analysis seeds bound measurement noise, not training variance. These are demonstrations of a direction, not effect sizes.
  \item \textbf{Scale, and in the unhelpful direction.} 0.5B throughout; the 1.5B replication holds (AUROC $0.974$) but the applied gain \emph{shrinks}, $+8.6$ against $+11.7$\,pp. One task, one model family, one RL algorithm --- and the judge is a bystander, not the optimisation target.
  \item \textbf{A withdrawn result.} An earlier version reported that RL renders the probe direction causally active under activation steering. We do not: the steered vector has cosine $0.163$ with the probe actually optimized rather than the $1.000$ claimed, the intervention landed one transformer block and 2--3 tokens downstream of the read site, and the key contrasts reach only $p=0.063$. Those checkpoints are deleted.
  \item \textbf{Reproducibility.} Every number regenerates on CPU from released artifacts; one script prints the published value beside each recomputed one and exits non-zero on disagreement.
\end{itemize}
